'''Cobham Limited''' is a British aerospace  manufacturing company based in [[Bournemouth]], England.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Cobham, Home|url=https://www.cobham.com/|access-date=2021-12-17|website=www.cobham.com}}</ref> Founded by Sir [[Alan Cobham]] as '''Flight Refuelling Limited''' (FRL) in 1934, the company has since grown and diversified into various markets through its acquisitions. 

During 1994, the firm was formally renamed Cobham plc; by this point, the company had in excess of 10,000 employees and had operations in [[North America]], [[Europe]], [[Malaysia]] and [[South Africa]]. In January 2020, the company was acquired by [[United States|American]] [[private equity firm]] [[Advent International]] for £4 billion, and Cobham Mission Systems, its aerial refuelling wing, was sold to [[Eaton Corporation|Eaton]] in June 2021 for $2.83 billion.

==History==
===1930s to 1990s: Formation, early activities and growth===
During the 1920s and 1930s, [[Aerial refueling#Early experiments|aerial refuelling]] of aircraft in mid-flight was performed only on an experimental basis, typically for attempts to set new flight endurance records.<ref name = "cobham heritage"/> During this era, [[Alan Cobham]] became an accomplished pilot, winning multiple air races as well as the [[de Havilland]] aircraft company appointing him as their senior pilot.<ref name=michael/> Cobham decided to leave de Havilland to pursue his own ventures, including the formation of an [[Aerobatics|aerobatic troupe]] and a small airline; he embarked on a long term campaign to popularize commercial air travel, making efforts to secure both public and the British Government's backing for the sector.<ref name = "cobham heritage">{{cite web |url = http://www.cobhaminvestors.com/our-business/our-hertitage |title = Our Heritage |publisher = Cobham |access-date = 15 December 2019 |archive-date = 1 February 2020 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200201165230/http://www.cobhaminvestors.com/our-business/our-hertitage |url-status = dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.historyhit.com/who-was-sir-alan-cobham-the-man-who-brought-aviation-to-the-masses/ |title = Who Was Sir Alan Cobham? The Man Who Brought Aviation to the Masses |publisher = historyhit.com |date = 26 March 2019 |first = Colin |last = Cruddas}}</ref>

[[File:IFR Canberra.jpg|thumb|[[English Electric Canberra]] of Flight Refuelling Ltd]]
Cobham believed that practical in-flight refuelling techniques would revolutionise commercial airlines and enable new long distance air routes; however, development work later focused largely upon its military applications.<ref name=michael/> He founded a new company, known as Flight Refuelling Limited (FRL), in 1934 that was initially headquartered at [[RAF Ford]] in [[Sussex]].<ref name=michael>{{cite web |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/1516495/Sir-Michael-Cobham.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/1516495/Sir-Michael-Cobham.html |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title=Obituary: Sir Michael Cobham |work=The Telegraph |date=24 April 2006 |access-date=26 March 2015}}{{cbignore}}</ref> 

During 1939, the company played a role in several non-stop crossings of the Atlantic performed by British airline [[Imperial Airways]];<ref name = "Cobham timeline">{{cite web |url = http://www.cobhaminvestors.com/~/media/Files/C/Cobham-IR-V2/documents/our-heritage-timeline.pdf |title = Cobham - Timeline |publisher = Cobham |access-date = 15 December 2019 }}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> yet, the adoption of aerial refuelling by the [[United States Air Force]] during the initial [[post-war]] years most prominently highlighted the company's technological value.<ref name = "cobham heritage"/> 

During 1947, the company relocated to [[RAF Tarrant Rushton|Tarrant Rushton]] in [[Dorset]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.theyetties.co.uk/shop980_cat159_tarrant_rushton_the_secret_airfield_history_war.htm |title=Tarrant Rushton – The Secret Airfield |access-date=16 March 2014}}</ref> From 1948-9, it was contracted to carry liquid fuel as part of the [[Berlin Airlift]], in what would be known as the 'Liquid Lift'.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Sweet Victory: How the Berlin Airlift Divided East and West|last=Pearson|first=Joseph|date=2025|publisher=Pegasus Books|isbn=9781639368587|location=New York}}</ref> During the late 1940s, the company's aerial refuelling equipment broke new ground, including a round-the-world flight by specially equipped [[Boeing B-50 Superfortress]]es in 1948 and the demonstration of the since-widely used [[Aerial refueling#Probe-and-drogue|'probe and drogue']] method of air-to-air refuelling for the first time in 1949.<ref name = "Cobham timeline"/> The [[Royal Air Force]] (RAF) would soon adopt the probe-and-drogue approach, as would various other international customers. Cobham's air-to-air refuelling system was perhaps most crucially used during the [[Falklands War]] of 1982, being used to facilitate the long-distance sorties of the RAF's [[Avro Vulcan]] bombers for [[Operation Black Buck]], successfully reaching and bombing the [[Argentina|Argentinian]]-held airfield at [[Port Stanley]] on the islands.<ref name = "cobham heritage"/>

During 1954, Michael Cobham, Alan's son, took a role in the company; he soon began to steer Cobham to diversify into new markets.<ref name = "cobham heritage"/> One such venture was the reorganising of Cobham Group's Airfield Services division into the newly incorporated FR Aviation, which saw contractor-owned and operated aircraft operate directly alongside military customers. Communications and electronics were other key sectors of interest.<ref name = "cobham heritage"/>

In 1963, the firm centred its manufacturing activity at its new site in [[Ashington, Dorset|Ashington]], [[Wimborne]] in Dorset.<ref name = "Cobham timeline"/> During 1969, Michael took over the leadership of the business from Alan; he remained as Cobham's chairman and chief executive through to the mid 1990s.<ref name=michael/>

During 1985, Cohbam became a [[public limited company]]; despite the [[initial public offering|stock flotation]], the Cobham family retained a large stake in the business.<ref name=michael/> As a consequence of various acquisitions and internal growth, Cobham developed various product lines across the aerospace market for both civilian and military, and thus its in-flight refuelling technology became a relatively small element of Cobham's portfolio over time.<ref name=michael/>

In 1994, the firm was formally renamed Cobham plc.<ref name = "cobham heritage"/> By this time, the company had in excess of 10,000 employees and had operations present in [[North America]], [[Europe]], [[Malaysia]] and [[South Africa]].<ref name=michael/>

===1990s to 2019: Acquisitions and disposals as a listed company===
In September 1997, Cobham acquired [[ML Aviation]] for £37 million, which had taken over [[Nash & Thompson]], a major competitor, the previous year.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://home.comcast.net/~aero51/html/history/mlaviation.htm | title = Aero History | publisher = Comcast}}.</ref>

In June 2001 Cobham acquired Sierra Flight Systems and merged it into its Chelton Avionics business, naming the combined division Chelton Flight Systems.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.flightglobal.com/general-aviation/2001/07/chelton-takes-sierra-flight-systems/ | title = Chelton takes Sierra Flight Systems |access-date = 3 August 2026 |date = 3 July 2001|publisher = Flight Global}}.</ref>

In early 2008, Cobham purchased [[S-TEC Corporation]], maker of general aviation autopilots, for $38 million;<ref>{{cite journal |title=Cobham buys S-TEC Corporation |journal=Flying Magazine |date=February 2008 |page = 24}}</ref> during February 2008, the company also bought the [[sensor]] and [[Antenna (radio)|antenna]] systems division of [[BAE Systems]] for $240 million.<ref>{{cite web | place = UK | url = http://www.theengineer.co.uk/Articles/304759/Cobham+buys+BAE+Systems+division.htm | archive-url = https://archive.today/20130505081346/http://www.theengineer.co.uk/Articles/304759/Cobham+buys+BAE+Systems+division.htm | url-status = dead | archive-date = 5 May 2013 | title = Cobham buys BAE Systems Division | newspaper = The Engineer | date = 25 February 2008 }}</ref> In June 2008, Cobham acquired [[Sparta Inc.]], a US defence business, for $416 million (it was renamed [[Cobham Analytic Solutions]]).<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.rfglobalnet.com/article.mvc/Cobham-To-Purchase-SPARTA-For-416-Million-0001 | title = Cobham to purchase Sparta for $416m | newspaper = RF Globalnet | date = 16 January 2008}}</ref> In September 2008 Cobham completed the purchase of the [[radio frequency]] components business of [[M/A-COM]] for $425 million.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://tycoelectronics.mediaroom.com/index.php?s=43&item=280 | title = Tyco Electronics Announces Agreement to Sell Its RF Components and Subsystem Business To Cobham Plc | publisher = Tyco | type = press release | date = 13 May 2008 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080210142406/http://tycoelectronics.mediaroom.com/index.php?s=43 | archive-date = 10 February 2008 }}</ref> In April 2009, Cobham agreed to purchase Argotek Inc., a provider of high-end [[information assurance]] services to the [[United States Intelligence Community]], for $36 million.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.theengineer.co.uk/news/cobham-buys-argotek/311491.article | title = Cobham buys Argotek | publisher = The Engineer | date = 22 May 2009 | access-date = 26 March 2015 }}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> In June 2009, a Cobham – [[Northrop Grumman]] 50–50 joint venture won the US Army's US$2.4 billion competition to supply Vehicular Intercom Systems.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.defense-aerospace.com/article-view/release/109762/northrop,-cobham-team-for-us-army%27s-vis_x-intercom.html | title = Northrop Grumman, Cobham Team to Resume Work on U.S. Army's VIS-X Vehicular Intercommunication System | publisher = Defence Aerospace | date =10 November 2009 |access-date=26 March 2015}}</ref>

In October 2011, Cobham Analytic Solutions was sold for $350 million to the privately owned [[Parsons Corporation]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2011-10-19/parsons-to-buy-systems-unit-from-cobham-for-350-million-1- | title = Parsons to Buy Systems Unit From Cobham for $350 Million | publisher =Bloomberg |date=19 October 2011 |access-date=26 March 2015}}</ref> Then in June 2012, Cobham acquired Danish satellite communications company Thrane & Thrane A/S, making it the core of Cobham's new SATCOM [[strategic business unit]] (SBU), to include SeaTel marine, TracStar land and Omnipless airborne SATCOM product lines.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/transport/9243993/Cobham-ups-bid-to-secure-Thrane-and-Thrane.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/transport/9243993/Cobham-ups-bid-to-secure-Thrane-and-Thrane.html |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title=Cobham ups bid to secure Thrane & Thrane |date=3 May 2012 |work=The Telegraph |access-date=16 March 2014}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

In May 2013, Cobham acquired antenna systems business, Axell Wireless.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rcrwireless.com/article/20130521/networks/cobham-buys-das-provider-axell-wireless/ |title=Cobham buys DAS provider Axell Wireless |publisher=RCR Wireless |date=21 May 2013 |access-date=16 March 2014}}</ref> In July 2013, the company bought out FB Heliservices joint venture partner Bristow Helicopters.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/industry/10181351/Cobham-pays-50m-to-take-control-of-helicopter-firm-that-trained-princes.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/newsbysector/industry/10181351/Cobham-pays-50m-to-take-control-of-helicopter-firm-that-trained-princes.html |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title=Cobham pays £50m to take control of helicopter firm that trained princes |date=15 July 2013 |work=The Telegraph |access-date=16 March 2014}}{{cbignore}}</ref> In April 2014, Cobham sold [[Chelton Flight Systems]] and [[S-TEC Corporation]] to Genesys Aerosystems.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.flyingmag.com/news/cobham-sells-s-tec-and-chelton-flight-systems |title=Cobham Sells S-Tec and Chelton Flight Systems |work=Flying Magazine |date=22 April 2014 |access-date=26 March 2015 |archive-date=22 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210622005450/https://www.flyingmag.com/news/cobham-sells-s-tec-and-chelton-flight-systems/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Then in May 2014, Cobham acquired wireless communications company, [[Aeroflex]] Holding Corporation for $1.46 billion.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://dealbook.nytimes.com/2014/05/20/cobham-acquires-wireless-communications-company-for-1-46-billion/?_php=true&_type=blogs&_r=0 |title=Cobham Acquires Wireless Communications Company for $1.46 Billion |date=20 May 2014 |work=New York Times |access-date=20 May 2014}}</ref>

In August 2016, David Lockwood was named CEO, replacing Bob Murphy.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/u-k-defense-supplier-cobham-names-new-ceo-1471420601 |title=U.K. Defense Supplier Cobham Names New CEO |last1=Wall |first1=Robert |date=17 August 2016 |last2=Panchal |first2=Tapan |newspaper=Wall Street Journal |issn=0099-9660 |access-date=17 August 2016}}</ref>

===2019 onwards: Private equity ownership and further restructuring===

In July 2019, the company's board agreed to recommend a takeover offer of £4 billion from [[United States|American]] [[private equity firm]] [[Advent International]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ft.com/content/3e463652-ae6d-11e9-8030-530adfa879c2 |title=Cobham snapped up by US buyout group Advent in £4bn deal |date=25 July 2019 |publisher=FT.com |access-date=25 August 2019}}</ref> However, the bid was criticised by Cobham's largest shareholder, and the firm's chairman subsequently remarked that Cobham was seeking out alternative offers.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-08-03/cobham-seeking-alternatives-to-advent-offer-chairman-tells-ft |title = Cobham Is Seeking Alternatives to Advent Offer, Chairman Tells FT |publisher = Bloomberg |date = 3 August 2019 |first = Lucca de |last = Paoli}}</ref> In response, Advent issued several guarantees, seeking to mollify national security concerns ahead of pending approval of the deal by the British Government.<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/2019/10/29/advent-ready-offer-cobham-guarantees-deadline-looms/ |title = Advent ready to offer Cobham guarantees as UK decision looms |work = The Telegraph|first = Alan |last = Tovey |date = 29 October 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/2019/11/19/cobham-deal-set-go-ahead-leadsom-accepts-advent-promises/ |title = Leadsom under fire over national security risks as she signals Cobham deal will go ahead |work = The Telegraph|first = Alan |last = Tovey |date = 19 November 2019}}</ref> The UK Conservative government approved the takeover in December 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-50874181|title=UK approves £4bn US takeover of defence company Cobham|publisher=BBC|date=21 December 2019|access-date=21 December 2019}}</ref> The transaction was completed on 17 January 2020.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.investegate.co.uk/article.aspx?id=202001170958091697A|title=Scheme becomes effective|publisher=Investigate|date=17 January 2020|access-date=17 January 2020}}</ref> The communications division was sold off in November 2020 to TransDigm Group Inc. for $965 million.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.themiddlemarket.com/latest-news/transdigm-acquires-cobham-aero-connectivity-for-965m|title=TransDigm Acquires Cobham Aero Connectivity for $965M|website=Mergers & Acquisitions|date=24 November 2020 }}</ref>

After 18 months, Advent had already sold the bulk of Cobham's operations to other buyers, leaving it with no UK manufacturing operations.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/2021/08/17/unions-warn-us-feeding-frenzy-british-defence-industry/ |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/2021/08/17/unions-warn-us-feeding-frenzy-british-defence-industry/ |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=Unions warn of US 'feeding frenzy' over British defence industry|first=Alan|last=Tovey|newspaper=The Telegraph |date=17 August 2021|via=www.telegraph.co.uk}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

In September 2020, [[Draken International]] purchased Cobham Aviation Services based in [[Bournemouth]] and [[Teesside International Airport]], and renamed it Draken Europe. Cobham's 15 [[Dassault Falcon 20]] aircraft, were added to Draken's fleet.<ref name="Draken Europe">{{cite web |title=Draken Europe Launches Brand |url=https://www.draken.aero/news/draken-europe-launches-brand/ |website=Draken Europe |access-date=18 May 2021 |archive-date=23 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230323043153/https://www.draken.aero/news/draken-europe-launches-brand/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Donald |first=David |title=Draken Buys Cobham's Falcon Fleet; ATAC Lands Eglin Deal |url=https://www.ainonline.com/aviation-news/defense/2020-09-30/draken-buys-cobhams-falcon-fleet-atac-lands-eglin-deal |access-date=2022-04-08 |website=Aviation International News |language=en}}</ref>

On 1 June 2021, Eaton completed their acquisition of Cobham Mission Systems for $2.83 billion, 14 times the company's 2020 earnings.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-cobham-mission-systems-m-a-eaton-corp-idUSKBN2A12EL|title=Eaton to buy Cobham Mission Systems in $2.83 billion deal|newspaper=Reuters |date=1 February 2021|via=www.reuters.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.eaton.com/us/en-us/company/news-insights/news-releases/2021/eaton-completes-acquisition-of-cobham-mission-systems-.html|title=Eaton completes acquisition of Cobham Mission Systems|date=1 June 2021|publisher=Eaton Inc|access-date=13 May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=February 3, 2021 |title=Cobham aerial refuelling wing sold to Eaton|url=https://www.airforce-technology.com/news/cobham-aerial-refuelling/|work=Airforce Technology}}</ref>

In August 2021, the British aerospace and defence company, Cobham proposed a £2.6 billion purchase of [[Ultra Electronics]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-58228657 |title=UK defence giant Ultra agrees to £2.6bn Cobham takeover |website=BBC |date=16 August 2021 |access-date=3 August 2026}}</ref> As the latter was a key national security and defence contractor and Cobham was American-owned at the time, the acquisition was the subject of a national security review. In July 2022, the UK government approved the transaction subject to undertakings by Cobham and Ultra.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Update on the proposed acquisition of Ultra Electronics Holdings plc by Cobham Ultra Acquisitions Limited |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/news/update-on-the-proposed-acquisition-of-ultra-electronics-holdings-plc-by-cobham-ultra-acquisitions-limited |access-date=2025-07-03 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref>

In July 2023, French multinational [[Thales Group]] entered into a deal to acquire the aerospace communications business of Cobham for $1.1 billion, which completed during the first half of 2024.<ref>{{cite news |last=Aleksandrowicz |first=Michal |date=12 July 2023 |title=Thales to buy Cobham Aerospace Communications for $1.1 billion |url=https://www.reuters.com/markets/deals/thales-acquire-cobham-aerospace-communications-11-billion-2023-07-12/ |publisher=Reuters}}</ref>

In 2025, it was announced that US-based power solutions manufacturer [[Eaton Corporation]] had agreed to buy Ultra PCS Limited from Cobham Ultra Group for $1.55 billion.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eaton to Buy U.K.’s Ultra PCS in $1.55B Aerospace Deal |url=https://www.mdm.com/news/top-distributor-sectors/electrical/eaton-to-buy-u-k-s-ultra-pcs-in-1-55b-aerospace-deal/ |access-date=2026-08-03 |website=Modern Distribution Management |language=en}}</ref> The deal completed in January 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eaton completes acquisition of Ultra PCS Limited, expanding capabilities and solutions for next-generation aerospace and defense markets |url=https://www.eaton.com/us/en-us/company/news-insights/news-releases/2026/eaton-completes-acquisition-of-ultra-pcs-limited.html |access-date=2025-08-03 |website=Eaton Corporation|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Eaton completes acquisition of Ultra PCS Limited, expanding capabilities and solutions for next-generation aerospace and defense markets |url=https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260123202659/en/Eaton-completes-acquisition-of-Ultra-PCS-Limited-expanding-capabilities-and-solutions-for-next-generation-aerospace-and-defense-markets |access-date=2025-08-03 |website=Business Wire|language=en}}</ref>

In June 2026, it was announced that [[Booz Allen Hamilton]] had agreed to acquire the Ultra I&C Mission Solutions business (Ultra Mission Solutions) for $720 million. Ultra Mission Solutions is a division within Ultra I&C specialising in mission‑critical software, encryption, and edge‑compute products.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Booz Allen to Acquire Ultra I&C Mission Solutions Business, Further Strengthening Defense Technology Portfolio |url=https://www.ultra-ic.com/newsroom/news/booz-allen-to-acquire-ultra-ic-mission-solutions-business-further-strengthening-defense-technology-portfolio/ |access-date=2025-08-03 |website=Ultra I&C|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Booz Allen to Acquire Ultra I&C Mission Solutions Business, Further Strengthening Defense Technology Portfolio |url=https://markets.ft.com/data/announce/detail?dockey=600-202606220800BIZWIRE_USPRX____20260622_BW758452-1 |access-date=2025-08-03 |website=Financial Times|language=en}}</ref>

==Operations==

As of August 2026, Cobham is organised into three strategic business units:

* Ultra Maritime: focused on undersea warfare solutions<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://umaritime.com/ |title=Cobham Ultra Maritime |publisher=Cobham Ultra Group  |access-date=3 August 2026}}</ref>
* Ultra I&C: focused on crypto solutions, mission software and tactical communications for defence applications<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ultra-ic.com/ |title=Cobham Ultra I&C |publisher=Cobham Ultra Group |access-date=3 August 2026}}</ref>
* C16 Ventures: makes early stage and growth equity investments within space, aerospace and defence<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://c16ventures.com/ |title=C16 Ventures|publisher=Cobham Ultra Group  |access-date=3 August 2026}}</ref>

==Products==
The company produces the Guardian ST820, a battery-operated tracking device used by the American [[intelligence agency]] [[FBI]]. The device, which is only available to law enforcement entities, can be secured underneath a car by a strong magnet and incorporates a [[GPS]] receiver.<ref>{{cite web |last = Rothman |first = Wilson |url = https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna39583860 |title = FBI busted tracking student, demands GPS spy gear returned |work = [[NBC News]] |date = 8 October 2010}}</ref>

In his 2015 book Data and Goliath, American security expert [[Bruce Schneier]] wrote that Cobham sells a system enabling buyers to send "blind calls" to mobile phones: calls that don't ring, and are undetectable by the recipient. As described by Schneier, the blind call allows the sender to track the phone's location to within one metre. Schneier noted that Cobham's customers include the governments of [[Algeria]], [[Brunei]], [[Ghana]], [[Pakistan]], [[Saudi Arabia]], [[Singapore]] and the [[United States]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Schneier |first=Bruce |title=Data and Goliath: The Hidden Battles to Collect Your Data and Control Your World |date=2015 |publisher=W.W. Norton and Company |location=New York |isbn=978-0393244816}}<!--|access-date=17 March 2015--></ref>

===Rebreathers===
Carleton Life Support, a subsidiary of Cobham based in [[Davenport, Iowa]], US makes the MK 16 [[rebreather]] used by the [[United States Navy]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kmimediagroup.com/special-operations-technology/articles/334-special-operations-technology/sotech-2011-volume-9-issue-5-july/4472-diving-gear-sp-472 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402112525/http://www.kmimediagroup.com/special-operations-technology/articles/334-special-operations-technology/sotech-2011-volume-9-issue-5-july/4472-diving-gear-sp-472 |url-status=usurped |archive-date=2 April 2015 |title=Diving gear |publisher=Special Operations Technology |date=13 July 2011 |access-date=26 March 2015}}</ref> and the Siva range of [[diving rebreather]]s, originally made by Fullerton Sherwood Engineering.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/tr/pdf/ADA371173.pdf|title=Navy Experimental Diving Unit|publisher=Department of the Navy|access-date=5 March 2024}}</ref>

====Siva====
<!-- target for redirect [[Siva (rebreather)]] -->
The versions of Siva are:<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cobhammissionsystems.com/safety-and-survival/military-dive-rebreathers/|title=Rebreathers|publisher=Cobham|access-date=20 May 2021}}</ref>
* Siva S10 oxygen rebreather, with a dive duration rated as 4 hours, which is worn on the chest.
* Siva S24, a dual mode oxygen or semi-closed circuit mixed gas rebreather with maximum operating depth normally limited to 24 metres, but can be set to 55 metres, which is worn on the chest.
* Siva-55 is worn on the back. It has two 200 bar [[Inconel]] spheres with a total volume of 5.6 litres. It is superseded by the Carleton Viper<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.therebreathersite.nl/SemiClosed%20Rebreathers/Canada/carleton_siva_55.htm |title=Carleton Siva 55 |website=www.therebreathersite.nl|accessdate=21 May 2021}}</ref> The Siva 55, also known as Canadian Clearance Diving Apparatus (CCDA), is rated for an operating depth up to 55 metres. It can be used as a semi-closed circuit rebreather with any one of 3 standard [[nitrox]] mixes (32.5, 40 and 60% oxygen) or as a closed circuit oxygen rebreather.
* Siva+ is worn on the back. It is also known as Canadian Underwater Mine-countermeasure Apparatus ([[CUMA]]). It is a self-mixing rebreather which works on the principle of a flow of oxygen which is mixed with a diluent to a ratio dependent on the ambient pressure. The Siva+ is rated for 90 metres. The diluent can be air or [[Trimix (breathing gas)|trimix]] or [[heliox]].

====Viper====
[[File:Viper SC rebreather Kotka 2013.JPG|thumb|Viper-SC rebreather]]
Viper is an electronically controlled [[Rebreather#Fully closed circuit rebreather|closed circuit mixed gas rebreather]] originally manufactured by Carleton Life Support, subsequently acquired by Cobham plc and fitted with the Juergensen Defense Corporation Mark V Electronic Control System. It is designed for use by combat [[Explosive Ordnance Disposal]] divers, and for diving to remove [[naval mine]]s which may be sensitive to sound and magnetic fields. The technology is derived from the Carleton SIVA 55 rebreathers. It is worn in a [[Backplate and wing|back inflation buoyancy compensator harness]] which incorporates two [[counterlung]]s, one on each side. All of its components are on the back, exposed. It can use a [[Mouthpiece (scuba)|mouthpiece]] or a variety of [[fullface mask]]s. It is designed to be silent and non-magnetic. The front of the wearer is clear, enabling the user to climb in and out of boats and over walls. The Viper has a large cylindrical [[scrubber canister]] longitudinally on the back, two spherical gas containers side by side below that, and optionally, a [[bailout cylinder]] set transversely underneath. It uses a [[Loop rebreather|loop configuration]] breathing circuit. Three versions of the Viper are made:<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.berufstaucher.at/viper_e_underwater_mine_countermeasures_diving_apparatus.pdf|title=Underwater Mine Countermeasures (MCM) Diving Apparatus|publisher=Berufstaucher|access-date=7 April 2026}}</ref>

*Viper SC Underwater Mine Countermeasures (MCM) Diving Apparatus
*Viper Plus
*Viper E Mixed Gas Underwater Breathing Apparatus

==Queen's Awards for Enterprise==
* 2007: Cobham Defense Communications, based in [[Blackburn]], [[Lancashire]], received a Queen's Award for Enterprise in the International Trade category. The business was awarded the award for its ability to supply leading edge intercom systems to customers around the world.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.army-technology.com/contractors/navigation/cobham-defence/ |title=Cobham Defence Communications |work=Army Technology |access-date=1 May 2018 |language=en-GB}}</ref> 
* 2009: Cobham Surveillance, based in [[Segensworth]], [[Hampshire]], England, received a Queen's Award for Enterprise in the International Trade category.  The business – formerly known as Domo Ltd – tripled its export sales in three years.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.microwavejournal.com/articles/8416-cobham-surveillance-receives-queen-s-award-for-exports | title =Cobham Surveillance Receives Queen's Award for Exports |date=8 September 2009 |publisher=Microwave Journal |access-date=26 March 2015}}</ref>
* 2010: Cobham Surveillance, based in [[Segensworth]], [[Hampshire]], received a Queen's Award for Enterprise in the Innovation category.  The award was for the development of its Solo4 wireless digital audio and video link technology that improves safety for bomb disposal teams and law enforcement personnel by increasing the range at which they can effectively operate their robotic bomb disposal equipment.<ref name="cobham.com">{{cite web | url = http://www.dailyecho.co.uk/business/8113649.print/ | title = Queen's Awards for five Hampshire firms |publisher=Daily Echo |date=22 April 2010 |access-date=26 March 2015}}</ref>
* 2010: Cobham Antenna Systems, based in [[Marlow, Buckinghamshire]], received a Queen's Award for Enterprise in the International Trade category. The business – formerly known as Chelton Ltd – continuously increased export revenues over six years and sells over 80% of its production overseas.<ref name="cobham.com" />

==Sports club==
The company created Cobham Sports and Social Club, a members' club in [[Merley]] near the main manufacturing site in [[Wimborne, Dorset]] in 1971.  Whilst this club is no longer part of Cobham, it still uses the Cobham branding and is used as the ground for [[Merley Cobham Sports F.C.]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.thedpl.co.uk/thedpl/clubs/merley-cobham.html |title=Dorset Premier League |work=thedpl.co.uk |access-date=26 March 2015 |archive-date=18 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220818125824/http://thedpl.co.uk/thedpl/clubs/merley-cobham.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

extract:
Cobham Limited is a British aerospace  manufacturing company based in Bournemouth, England. Founded by Sir Alan Cobham as Flight Refuelling Limited (FRL) in 1934, the company has since grown and diversified into various markets through its acquisitions. 
During 1994, the firm was formally renamed Cobham plc; by this point, the company had in excess of 10,000 employees and had operations in North America, Europe, Malaysia and South Africa. In January 2020, the company was acquired by American private equity firm Advent International for £4 billion, and Cobham Mission Systems, its aerial refuelling wing, was sold to Eaton in June 2021 for $2.83 billion.
